query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with an FCC matrix, elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., 900–1100 K) in oxidizing atmospheres leads to selective oxidation at surface defects and grain boundaries, forming a stratified (e.g., Ni-/Cr-/Fe-rich) oxide scale whose growth stresses suppress conventional dislocation slip and promote a local transformation of the FCC matrix to a brittle phase (such as a BCC/intermetallic structure). Conversely, in reducing atmospheres where oxidation is minimized, diffusion-driven precipitation of brittle secondary phases (e.g., Cr-rich σ phases) at grain boundaries dominates. Both processes yield a significant reduction (on the order of 30–50% relative to the as-built baseline) in ductility and strength and trigger catastrophic failure when a critical threshold of oxide scale thickness or precipitate volume fraction is exceeded.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy in a supersaturated, defect-rich FCC state with fine grain structure.
generation.intervention: Expose nominally identical alloy samples to controlled elevated temperatures (900–1100 K) under well-defined oxidizing (e.g., high oxygen partial pressure) versus reducing (e.g., low or negligible oxygen partial pressure) gas atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Temperature maintained between 900–1100 K for variable durations (e.g., 50–200 hours) with gas compositions precisely controlled (e.g., O2-rich vs. forming gas such as H2/N2 mixture) while mechanical stresses are minimal (static exposure) prior to post-exposure characterization.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a layered oxide scale at surface regions and grain boundaries (in oxidizing conditions) or the nucleation of brittle intergranular precipitates (in reducing conditions).
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing environments, selective oxidation at high-energy sites leads to the accumulation of a stratified oxide scale whose internal growth stresses impede dislocation motion, thus forcing a transition from ductile FCC deformation to brittle phase formation, while in reducing environments, enhanced elemental diffusion promotes the precipitation of brittle secondary phases that weaken grain boundary cohesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-built baseline, samples exposed in oxidizing conditions will exhibit observable oxide scale growth (measurable by TEM/EDS) with corresponding suppression of dislocation activity (assessed via in situ straining or post-mortem fractography) and premature failure at lower strains; in reducing environments, microstructural analysis will reveal extensive intergranular brittle phase precipitation, with similar reductions in mechanical ductility and strength. Failure occurs once oxide scale thickness or precipitate volume fraction exceeds a critical threshold (e.g., oxide scale > tens of nm or precipitates >10% area fraction).
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured alloy exhibits a supersaturated, ductile FCC matrix with high toughness and uniform dislocation activity under room temperature mechanical loading.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for exposure conditions at elevated temperatures between approximately 900–1100 K and for gas atmospheres that are distinctly oxidizing (high O2 partial pressure) or reducing (e.g., forming gas). Deviations outside these boundaries may invoke additional degradation mechanisms (e.g., creep or grain growth) not considered here.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative thresholds for oxide scale thickness or precipitate volume fraction triggering catastrophic failure are not firmly established; variations in internal defect density and manufacturing residual stresses may also modulate the observed degradation rates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples and expose them separately to (a) an oxidizing gas environment (e.g., 21% O2 in N2) and (b) a reducing/oxygen-lean environment (e.g., 5% H2 in N2) at 900–1100 K for identical durations. After exposure, perform detailed microstructural (TEM, SEM/EDS) and mechanical (tensile, fracture toughness) testing. Additionally, use in situ high-temperature XRD to monitor phase evolution during exposure.
measurements: Quantitative oxide scale thickness and composition at surfaces and grain boundaries
Fraction and size distribution of any secondary (brittle) precipitates measured via microscopy
Mechanical properties (ductility, tensile strength, fracture strain)
Dislocation activity indicators through post-mortem analysis or in situ straining experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If altering the atmospheric condition (oxidizing vs. reducing) does not produce statistically significant differences in the type, extent, or distribution of surface oxidation or intergranular precipitate formation, or if the mechanical degradation (ductility and fracture behavior) does not correlate with the predicted microstructural changes, then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition. Another critical factor leading to the high ductility is the formation of nanovoids in the BCC lamellae during the latter stage of plastic deformation, which turns out to prevent catastrophic failure. In SEM observation (Fig. 5a), nanovoids (~100 nm in diameter) form within the BCC lamellae at a strain of 10%, initiating from the phase boundaries. With increasing strain (15–20%), more nanovoids appear and propagate within the BCC lamellae. Instead of causing rapid rupture of the lamellae, these nanovoids grow under the confinement of the adjacent FCC lamellae (already hardened at this stage), which effectively delays the failure of the alloy. At the final stage of deformation, the coalescence of these nanovoids breaks the constraints of the FCC lamellae, resulting in the fracture of the EHEA (Supplementary Fig. 8a).

cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 presents the mechanical stability analysis of the oxide scales. As shown in Figure 6, the cyclic oxidation results reveal pronounced differences in spallation resistance among the three alloys. The Base Alloy undergoes severe oxide-scale spallation after 100 thermal cycles at 1000 °C, resulting in substantial mass loss. The Synergy Alloy shows improved cyclic oxidation resistance, but measurable scale degradation still occurs. In contrast, the Innovation Alloy exhibits a mass change of only 0.05 ± 0.02 mg/cm2 after 100 cycles, with almost no detectable spallation, demonstrating excellent scale stability under thermal cycling. The simulated stress evolution further indicates that the oxide scale on the Innovation Alloy accumulates growth stress more slowly and can more effectively accommodate stress through local deformation and defect healing. Scratch testing confirms this enhanced interfacial stability: the critical load and interfacial fracture energy reach 78 N and 14.8 J/m2, respectively, which are substantially higher than those of the Synergy Alloy. The high entropy alloy (HEA) of equiatomic composition CrNiFeCoMn and with FCC crystal structure was additively manufactured in a selective laser melting (SLM) process starting from mechanically alloyed powders. The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K. The precipitates increase in number and dimensions after long-period annealing at 900–1300 K, with a change in the HEA mechanical properties. Higher aging temperatures in the furnace, above 1300 K, turn the alloy into a single FCC structure, with the disappearance of the nitride and σ phase precipitates inside the grains and at the grain boundaries, but still with the presence of a finer Cr-rich nitride precipitation phase. These results suggest that the as-produced HEA is a supersaturated solid solution at low and intermediate temperature with nitrides and σ nanostructures.

AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. papers.title: Microstructural Study of CrNiCoFeMn High Entropy Alloy Obtained by Selective Laser Melting.
papers.system: Equiatomic CrNiCoFeMn high‐entropy alloy produced by selective laser melting (SLM); predominantly FCC solid solution with fine nitride and σ‐phase precipitates at higher temperatures.
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying of powders followed by SLM and subsequent annealing at various temperatures (723–1423 K) with optical, SEM, and EDS analyses.
papers.findings: At lower annealing temperatures (up to ~923 K) the alloy remains a supersaturated FCC solid solution with fine precipitates at grain boundaries; above ~1023 K recrystallization occurs and a distinct Cr-rich σ phase emerges along with increased precipitate size.
papers.mechanism: Elevated-temperature diffusion facilitates precipitation (nitrides and σ phase) at grain boundaries, which could deteriorate the mechanical integrity of the alloy through local compositional changes and embrittlement.

papers.title: Mechanisms of chemical-reaction-induced tensile deformation of an Fe/Ni/Cr alloy revealed by reactive atomistic simulations.
papers.system: FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy tested under tensile deformation in vacuum versus in a simulated corrosive high-temperature/pressure water environment.
papers.approach: Atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations comparing deformation in vacuum to that in a chemically reactive environment.
papers.findings: In vacuum, deformation proceeds via generation of layered HCP phases from Shockley partial dislocations; under corrosive conditions, oxidation of the alloy surface suppresses Shockley partial formation and favors an FCC-to-BCC phase transition leading to premature loss of ductility.
papers.mechanism: Chemical reactions with the environment modify the surface chemistry such that oxidation suppresses normal dislocation mechanisms and induces a brittle phase transformation (from FCC to BCC), thereby reducing ductility.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high‐entropy alloy exposed to an oxidizing environment at 400 °C under low oxygen pressure (10 mbar).
papers.approach: In situ oxidation experiments with time-series TEM observations, ex situ TEM, XRD, and compositional profiling.
papers.findings: A layered oxide scale forms sequentially—starting with a Ni-enriched pre-oxide layer, followed by a Cr2O3-rich intermediate layer, and an outer layer enriched with Fe, Mn, and Co—after as little as 2 minutes of oxidation.
papers.mechanism: Element-specific oxidation kinetics driven by differences in oxidation potentials lead to sequential, stratified oxide formation; these compositional layering and the resulting interfacial stress gradients could promote scale spallation and substrate degradation.

papers.title: Unraveling the Superior High-Temperature Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCuAl-Based High-Entropy Alloys: Roles of Cr, Co, and Mn Alloying Additions.
papers.system: FeNiCuAl-based high-entropy alloy under cyclic oxidation conditions at 1000 °C, with comparisons among alloys differing by minor alloying (e.g., trace Y additions).
papers.approach: Cyclic thermal oxidation tests with oxidation cycling, stress evolution simulations, and scratch testing to probe oxide-scale adherence and spallation resistance.
papers.findings: The “Innovation Alloy” with trace Y addition exhibits minimal oxide-scale spallation and a very low mass change after 100 cycles, correlating with slower oxide growth stress accumulation and better interfacial stability compared to reference alloys.
papers.mechanism: Minor alloying additions (e.g., Y) enhance the mechanical stability of the oxide/alloy interface by accommodating growth stresses through localized deformation and healing, reducing scale spallation that normally leads to degradation.

established: Additively manufactured HEAs display supersaturated FCC matrices with high dislocation densities and microstructural defects that can serve as sites for oxidation and phase precipitation during thermal exposure.

Elevated-temperature exposure promotes diffusion‐controlled phase transformations (e.g., nitride and σ-phase precipitation) and oxide scale formation, which are known to affect mechanical performance.
Oxidation in HEAs is governed by element-specific reactivities, leading to layered oxide structures whose stability can directly affect the alloy’s degradation behavior.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermal annealing and microstructural analysis in additively manufactured HEAs to observe precipitation and phase changes.
approaches_tried.outcome: Identification of fine nitride/σ-phase precipitates and recrystallization above a critical temperature; provided insight into diffusion- and temperature-driven degradation.

approaches_tried.approach: Reactive atomistic tensile simulations under corrosive (oxidizing) versus inert conditions.
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed that oxidation can suppress beneficial dislocation mechanisms and induce a brittle phase transformation, suggesting a potential route for degradation.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ TEM and XRD studies of oxidation to monitor layered oxide formation.
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated rapid stratification in oxide scale growth, reinforcing the role of element-specific oxidation kinetics in degradation.

approaches_tried.approach: Cyclic high-temperature oxidation tests with tailored minor alloying additions.
approaches_tried.outcome: Showed that trace element additions can significantly improve oxide-scale adhesion and stability, mitigating degradation.

mechanisms: Elevated temperature accelerates diffusion leading to precipitation of secondary phases (e.g., σ-phase, nitrides) that degrade the structural integrity.
Oxidation-induced modification of dislocation behavior; surface oxidation can suppress conventional slip (Shockley partials) and trigger a phase transformation (FCC-to-BCC) that is more brittle.
Formation of layered oxide scales due to element-specific oxidation kinetics, where differential growth stresses at interfaces can promote spallation and catastrophic failure.
Minor alloying (e.g., Y addition) improves oxide/alloy interfacial bonding, thereby enhancing cyclic oxidation resistance by reducing spallation.
disagreements: The role of Al in oxidation is debated; some evidence indicates that Al may have a minor effect on the oxidation behavior of Ni and Co, while other studies emphasize its importance in forming protective scales.

There is variation regarding the phase transformation under oxidizing conditions – some studies report an FCC-to-HCP transformation while others show a shift to a brittle BCC phase, likely influenced by specific alloy chemistries and environmental conditions.
open_questions: For the specific AM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an FCC matrix, does the degradation primarily result from oxidation-induced suppression of dislocation activity or from diffusion-driven precipitation of brittle secondary phases?
How do oxidizing versus reducing gas environments distinctly influence the competition between protective oxide scale formation and deleterious phase transformations in this alloy?
What role do pre-existing internal defects and residual stresses from additive manufacturing play in accelerating surface oxidation or phase precipitation during high-temperature exposure?
What exposure boundaries (temperature, gas composition, and duration) delineate the regimes between gradual degradation and catastrophic failure?
opportunities: Conduct controlled thermal exposure experiments on additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 under both oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres to monitor microstructural evolution via in situ TEM and SEM.

Implement systematic variation of gas compositions (e.g., oxygen partial pressures) to correlate oxide scale formation, dislocation dynamics, and phase transformation behavior with mechanical degradation.

Use atomistic and phase-field simulations to predict how subtle compositional adjustments or minor alloying additions (akin to Y addition) might stabilize the protective oxide scale or delay brittle phase formation.

Develop quantified fatigue or tensile testing protocols under elevated temperature conditions to establish a clear falsification criterion for the mechanistic hypothesis, such as identifying a threshold in oxide scale spallation or dislocation mobility change beyond which catastrophic failure occurs.

directions.direction: Oxidation‐induced dislocation suppression and brittle phase transformation
directions.type: Mechanism study & controlled gas environment test
directions.assessment: This direction posits that under oxidizing conditions, selective surface oxidation (especially at inherent defects and grain boundaries) suppresses normal dislocation slip and instead induces a local FCC-to-brittle phase (e.g., BCC/intermetallic) transformation. This mechanism is supported by atomistic simulations (e.g., PMC9969177) and offers a direct link between gas atmosphere, dislocation activity, and catastrophic failure. The intervention (varying oxygen partial pressure) is straightforward and the expected microstructural changes are measurable.

directions.direction: Diffusion‐driven precipitation of embrittling intergranular phases
directions.assessment: This approach considers that elevated temperatures promote diffusion, leading to precipitation of brittle phases (such as Cr-rich σ phases) along the grain boundaries. This introduces local compositional deviations that can reduce cohesion and cause rupture. Evidence from SLM studies (e.g., PMC9414008) supports the role of diffusion-induced phase transformation, and the experiment can be controlled by changing exposure time and temperature. However, it may not directly capture the role of gas chemistry differences.

directions.direction: Layered oxide scale formation with growth-stress induced spallation
directions.type: Surface and coating characterization under cyclic oxidation
directions.assessment: This direction highlights that oxidizing environments lead to the formation of stratified oxide scales (with compositional layering as seen in PMC11169556) that accumulate growth stresses. Spallation and cyclic breakdown of the oxide scale result in the exposure of fresh substrate and rapid degradation. Although promising, this mechanism may be challenging to separate from the underlying substrate transformations.

directions.direction: Role of additive manufacturing–induced defects in accelerating oxidation and phase decomposition
directions.assessment: This concept centers on the idea that the high density of internal defects and residual stresses from the additive manufacturing process act as preferred sites for oxidation or diffusion‐mediated precipitation. Although this is well known, isolating the contribution of these pre-existent defects from the ambient gas effects requires complex defect characterization and might complicate testing pathways.

directions.direction: Comparative study of oxidizing versus reducing gas environments affecting degradation paths
directions.type: Controlled gas atmosphere experiments combined with microstructural and mechanical testing
directions.assessment: This route directly exploits the difference between oxidizing and reducing environments. It hypothesizes that under oxidizing conditions, degradation is dominated by the formation and eventual spallation of a brittle oxide scale (and related dislocation suppression), whereas under reducing conditions the absence of a protective scale enhances diffusion and precipitation of embrittling phases along grain boundaries. Feasible exposure boundaries can be set, and differences in failure mode can be quantified, making this study both direct and informative.

choice.direction: Comparative study of oxidizing versus reducing gas environments affecting degradation paths
choice.why: This direction directly targets the open question by comparing how gas chemistry tunes the degradation mechanisms in the additively manufactured alloy. It allows a controlled change (gas composition) to reveal whether the dominant degradation pathway is driven by oxidation‐induced dislocation suppression and brittle phase transformation or by diffusion‐driven embedding of precipitates. This approach leverages supporting evidence from layered oxide formation (PMC11169556) and oxidation-induced changes in deformation mechanisms (PMC9969177), providing a clear, falsifiable route.
